answers.primary: A remote MCP server on the HTTP transport, added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` and authenticated per engineer through Claude Code's built-in OAuth 2.0 browser flow from `/mcp` (or `claude mcp login <name>`). This is the documented Sentry-style pattern: the server entry can be shared (project `.mcp.json` or a plugin) while each engineer's token is minted and stored locally.
answers.rejected_alternative: A local stdio MCP server (or a Bash/curl skill) wrapping the vendor's REST API with a shared API key passed via `--env` or a static `Authorization` header. Rejected because it needs exactly the long-lived shared credential the team wants to avoid, and configuring `headers.Authorization` makes Claude Code report a failed connection rather than falling back to OAuth.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the outcome for connection, token storage, refresh and retry: Claude Code performs the OAuth dance, stores tokens in the OS keychain or credentials file, refreshes on 401 and retries once. The model only owns whether it reaches for those tools instead of asking a human to paste a trace.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs out of process; the session's main context window receives only tool results (stack traces, issue payloads). With tool search on by default the tool schemas are deferred rather than preloaded, and MCP output warns above 10,000 tokens and is capped at 25,000 by default unless `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is raised.
answers.lifecycle: Claude Code connects the server at session start and marks it as needing authentication on 401/403; the browser sign-in is a one-time per-machine step whose token then refreshes automatically. It applies until the server is removed, toggled off in `/mcp`, or credentials are cleared with `claude mcp logout` / Clear authentication.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or unreachable server shows as needing auth or failed, its tools are unavailable, and Claude is told which server failed rather than acting as if it were never configured. The practical gaps are non-interactive runs (`claude -p` and Agent SDK have no `/mcp` panel, so the OAuth flow cannot run and someone must sign in from an interactive session first), and prompt-injection exposure because error payloads are untrusted external content.
answers.version_caveat: OAuth applies to HTTP servers only; SSE is deprecated and WebSocket is header-auth only. `claude mcp login`/`logout` requires v2.1.186+, no-browser URL fallback v2.1.191+, the re-authenticate notice v2.1.195+, and the non-interactive needs-auth reporting to Claude v2.1.196+. Servers without Dynamic Client Registration need `--client-id` and a fixed `--callback-port`.

answers.primary: An LSP plugin: install `typescript-lsp` from the official marketplace, or ship your own plugin with a `.lsp.json` mapping `.ts`/`.tsx` to `typescript-language-server`. Claude Code then pushes language-server diagnostics into Claude's context immediately after each edit and exposes go-to-definition, find-references, hover, symbols and call hierarchy as navigation instead of grep.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook that runs `tsc --noEmit` after every Write/Edit and feeds the output back. Rejected because it delivers diagnostics only, gives no symbol navigation, and re-typechecks the project on every single edit.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code starts and supervises the language server process, injects diagnostics automatically after edits, and provides navigation as a tool surface. The model owns only whether it acts on a reported error and whether it prefers navigation over grep.
answers.context_boundary: The language server is a separate long-lived subprocess. What crosses into the main session context window is the diagnostic text after each edit plus any navigation results the model requests, so every edit carries a small recurring token cost.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the plugin is enabled and the workspace has been trusted, runs for the session, restarts on crash up to `maxRestarts`, and stops on session end or plugin disable. Setting `diagnostics: false` keeps navigation while suppressing automatic diagnostic injection.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently: if the language server binary is missing, Claude Code records `Executable not found in $PATH` in the `/plugin` Errors tab and Claude just keeps grepping with no visible degradation. Monorepos generate false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics, large projects make the server memory-hungry, and when two enabled servers claim `.ts` only the first registered one starts.
answers.version_caveat: The plugin does not ship the binary: `npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript` is a prerequisite. `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require v2.1.205 or later, and before v2.1.205 setting either caused Claude Code to skip the server entirely with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`. LSP servers start only after workspace trust.

answers.primary: One plugin holding all four pieces (skills/commands for the review helpers and workflows, `hooks/hooks.json` for the edit-time automations, `.mcp.json` for the shared external-tool configuration), published through a team plugin marketplace, and referenced from each repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` using `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus `enabledPlugins`, with marketplace auto-update enabled.
answers.rejected_alternative: Standalone `.claude/` configuration copied into each repository (commands, agents, and hooks in `settings.json`). Rejected because there is no update channel: every repo drifts independently and changes must be hand-propagated.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns distribution and loading: fetching the marketplace, prompting for install on folder trust, running the hooks, and starting the MCP servers. The model owns only whether it invokes the review skills and workflow commands.
answers.context_boundary: Skills, agents and MCP tool definitions load into each engineer's main session context and cost tokens every turn, which the `/plugin` detail view surfaces as a Context cost estimate. Hooks and the MCP server run in their own processes; only their output crosses back into the window.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when a teammate trusts the repository folder: Claude Code prompts to install the declared marketplaces and plugins, components load at session start, and `/reload-plugins` applies mid-session changes. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or the repo entry is removed (removing a marketplace uninstalls its plugins).
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the install gate, because it is an offer rather than a mandate. A plugin that only the project's `.claude/settings.json` enables and that comes from an external source does not load until the engineer runs the install; Claude Code just reports it as not installed and prints the `claude plugin install` command. Auto-update also fires after startup with up to a ten-minute random delay, so a running session keeps the version it launched with until reload.
answers.version_caveat: The install-prompt-on-every-plugin-load-path behavior requires v2.1.195 or later. Auto-update is on by default only for official Anthropic marketplaces; third-party and local marketplaces default to off, though admins can set `"autoUpdate": true` on the `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` suppresses updates unless `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` is also set, and `strictKnownMarketplaces` can restrict which marketplaces are allowed.

answers.primary: Ship the compiled binary in the plugin's `bin/` directory at the plugin root. Executables placed there are added to the Bash tool's `PATH` while the plugin is enabled, so the CLI is invokable as a bare command inside any Bash tool call and composes normally with grep and jq, in every project, with no user PATH edits.
answers.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI as a bundled stdio MCP server exposing each subcommand as a tool. Rejected because MCP tools are structured tool invocations, not shell words: they cannot be piped into grep or jq, which is precisely the composition requirement here.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code injects the plugin's `bin/` into the PATH it hands the Bash tool. The model owns constructing correct invocations, and the permission system still gates each Bash call as usual.
answers.context_boundary: The binary runs in the Bash tool's subprocess, outside the model's context; only stdout and stderr cross back into the session window. The PATH change is scoped to Claude Code's Bash tool, not to the user's interactive shell or other processes.
answers.lifecycle: Available from the moment the plugin is loaded and enabled (session start, or after `/reload-plugins` if enabled mid-session) and for every Bash call in that session across all projects. It disappears when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly: a missing executable bit, a wrong shebang, or a binary built for another OS or architecture surfaces only as `command not found` from the shell, after which Claude improvises absolute paths. A single compiled binary is platform-specific, so one plugin copy will not serve mac, Linux and Windows teammates without per-platform builds. Bash permission rules also need to allow the command name or every call prompts.
answers.version_caveat: The docs list `bin/` as a plugin-root directory with no version gate stated beyond a Claude Code version that supports plugins, and there is no `bin` field in the manifest schema, so the directory must literally be `bin/` at the plugin root rather than a configurable path. Because `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes on update and the old directory is pruned about two weeks later, anything that hard-codes an absolute path to the binary needs `/reload-plugins` after an update.

answers.primary: Distribute the bundle as a plugin from a git-hosted marketplace and omit `version` from both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry. Claude Code then resolves the version from the git commit SHA of the plugin's source and treats every commit as a new version, so a merge is the release. Enable auto-update on the marketplace so it lands without user action.
answers.rejected_alternative: An explicit semver `version` in `plugin.json` with a CHANGELOG per release. Rejected because with `version` set, pushing commits is not enough: users only receive changes when the field is bumped and `/plugin update` otherwise reports already at the latest version, which is exactly the bookkeeping to be avoided.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness entirely. Version resolution, the cache-key comparison, and the background auto-update pass are Claude Code's; nothing here depends on the model behaving.
answers.context_boundary: The update machinery runs outside the model's context. Only the resulting components occupy the session window, and after a reload the newly loaded components announce themselves in appended content while the earlier history still reads from the prompt cache.
answers.lifecycle: Auto-update runs shortly after session startup with a random delay of up to ten minutes; the running session keeps its launched versions, and you are prompted to run `/reload-plugins` or pick them up at next launch. It stops on uninstall, on marketplace removal, or when `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` is set without `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and unpinned: everyone silently tracks HEAD, so a broken commit propagates to the whole team with no review gate and no version to roll back to. Each superseded version directory lingers in the cache as an orphan for about fourteen days. Auto-update also defaults to off for third-party and local marketplaces, so if nobody enables it the daily commits never reach anyone.
answers.version_caveat: Commit-SHA fallback applies only to `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources inside a git-hosted marketplace; `npm` sources and local directories outside a git repo resolve to `unknown` and never look updated. A `version` in `plugin.json` beats one in the marketplace entry, so both must be left unset. `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` keeps plugin updates flowing when Claude Code's own updater is disabled.

answers.primary: An HTTP-transport MCP server entry that uses `headersHelper` pointing at the SSO helper command (script path or inline shell). Claude Code runs the command at connection time and merges the JSON object it writes to stdout into the connection headers, so each connection carries a freshly minted short-lived token even though the service exposes no OAuth endpoints.
answers.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` block with `"Authorization": "Bearer ${TOKEN}"` relying on environment-variable expansion in `.mcp.json`. Rejected because the value is resolved once when the config loads and cannot be re-minted when the token expires part way through a session.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness executes the helper, merges its headers over any static ones, and on a 401 or 403 re-runs it, reconnects, and retries the call once. The helper script itself owns token minting and any caching, since Claude Code deliberately does none.
answers.context_boundary: The helper runs in its own shell process with a ten-second timeout, from the session's working directory (or the plugin root for a plugin-provided server). Only the resulting headers cross into the MCP connection; no token value ever enters the model's context window.
answers.lifecycle: It runs fresh on each connection, meaning session start and every reconnect, plus once more on the automatic 401/403 retry. It applies for as long as the server entry exists and the server is enabled; there is no scheduled refresh in between, so mid-session expiry is handled by the retry path rather than proactively.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on the connection but can thrash: if the helper exceeds ten seconds, emits non-JSON, or the freshly minted token is rejected on the retry too, the server is flagged as needing authentication and its tools vanish mid-session. With no caching, a slow SSO helper is re-invoked on every reconnect. `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.
answers.version_caveat: The automatic re-run-and-retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193 or later. For a plugin-provided server, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` substitution inside `headersHelper` and the plugin-root working directory require v2.1.195 or later (earlier versions passed the placeholder through literally). As of v2.1.207 a plugin `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` because the field is shell-parsed; put the value in `headers` or have the script read it from its own config.

answers.primary: A background monitor shipped with the plugin: a `monitors/monitors.json` entry at the plugin root such as `{"name": "error-log", "command": "tail -F ./logs/error.log", "description": "Application error log", "when": "always"}`. Claude Code starts it automatically whenever the plugin is active and delivers each stdout line to Claude as a session notification.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill instructing Claude to launch `tail -F` as a background Bash task. Rejected because it only runs once someone invokes the skill and depends on the model remembering to start and re-check it, which is exactly the 'without anyone asking' requirement it fails.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code spawns and supervises the process for the lifetime of the session and pushes every emitted line in as a notification. The model owns only how it reacts to those lines.
answers.context_boundary: The `tail` process runs outside the model's context, in the session working directory. Every stdout line crosses into the main session context as a notification, so a chatty log spends context window directly and continuously.
answers.lifecycle: With the default `when: "always"` it starts at session start and on plugin reload; `"on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>"` instead defers it to the first dispatch of that skill. It runs for the rest of the session, and disabling the plugin mid-session does not stop an already-running monitor: it stops when the session ends. Picking up a new plugin version's monitor requires a session restart, not `/reload-plugins`.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions and are skipped entirely on hosts where the Monitor tool is unavailable, so headless or hosted runs silently get nothing. A high-volume error log floods the context window, and a monitor whose command dies (missing file, a relative path resolved against the wrong working directory) produces silence that reads exactly like 'no errors'. They run unsandboxed at hook trust level.
answers.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental component declared under `experimental.monitors`; the manifest schema may change between releases, top-level declaration still works but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require the `experimental.*` placement. As of v2.1.207 a monitor command cannot reference `${user_config.*}` and monitor processes receive no `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` environment variables.

answers.primary: Pin the OAuth scopes in the server's MCP configuration: an `"oauth": { "scopes": "<read-only scopes>" }` object on the HTTP server entry in `.mcp.json`. This is the documented mechanism for restricting a server to a security-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more, and it constrains the token actually minted on each engineer's machine rather than constraining the assistant.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules (or a PreToolUse hook) blocking the server's write and admin tools by name. Rejected because that only stops the assistant from calling them: the credential sitting on the machine would still carry write authority, which is the exact distinction security asked for.
answers.enforcement_owner: Shared between the harness and the vendor's authorization server. Claude Code sends only the pinned `scope` parameter during authorization; the identity provider is what actually limits the issued token. The model has no role, which is the point.
answers.context_boundary: Scope configuration lives in the MCP config and the resulting token in secure storage (system keychain on macOS, credentials file otherwise). Neither crosses into the model's context window; only tool results do.
answers.lifecycle: Applies at the authorization flow: first sign-in and every re-authentication, including the automatic re-auth after a 403. `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and the scopes discovered at `/.well-known`. A token minted before the pin was added keeps its original grant, so existing engineers must `claude mcp logout` and sign in again for the restriction to take effect.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at the API boundary: a tool needing a scope outside the pinned set returns 403 `insufficient_scope`, and Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes instead of widening, so the write path stays dead until someone deliberately edits the config. The residual risk is upstream: the guarantee is only as strong as the provider's scope model, so a service that issues coarse-grained tokens or ignores the requested scope can still hand back an over-privileged credential. Verify against the token the provider actually issues.
answers.version_caveat: Requires the HTTP transport, since OAuth does not apply to stdio and WebSocket is header-auth only. As of v2.1.196 Claude Code stops requesting the full `scopes_supported` catalog when `oauth.scopes` is unset (that behavior was triggering `invalid_scope` rejections from providers advertising admin-only scopes), and it appends `offline_access` to the pinned set when the authorization server advertises it, so the pinned list is not literally the only scope requested. Metadata fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supplies `scopes_supported` when `oauth.scopes` is left unset.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: a `.mcp.json` at the repository root, committed to version control, added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> --scope project <url>`. It loads only in that project, arrives with a fresh clone, and Claude Code prompts each person for approval before it is ever used.
answers.rejected_alternative: Bundling the same server inside a team plugin. Rejected because plugin servers install per user across scopes and are a distribution channel aimed at many repositories, whereas project `.mcp.json` is the repository-bound mechanism that already carries the one-time per-user consent prompt.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code reads `.mcp.json`, holds the entry at pending approval until the user accepts, records the decision per user, and starts the connection. Nothing depends on the model.
answers.context_boundary: Scoped to sessions opened in that project directory. The server runs out of process and only tool results cross into the session window. Keep the credential out of the committed file by using `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` expansion, which works in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url`, and `headers`.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated at session start in that project. Approval is a one-time per-user decision that persists until reset with `claude mcp reset-project-choices`. It never loads in another project, and a local- or user-scoped server with the same name takes precedence over it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: until approved the server shows as pending approval and its tools do not exist, which can read to Claude as if the capability were never configured. A cloned repository cannot self-approve, so `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or `enabledMcpjsonServers` committed to `.claude/settings.json` is ignored until the workspace trust dialog is accepted. A missing environment variable does not block loading either: Claude Code warns and passes the literal `${VAR}` through, producing a confusing downstream auth failure.
answers.version_caveat: As of v2.1.196 `claude mcp list`/`get` read `.mcp.json` approvals from checked-in settings only after the workspace is trusted; before v2.1.207 an untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` could approve servers in a never-trusted folder. A JSON entry with a `url` must declare `"type"` explicitly or the server is skipped (the error message was clearer from v2.1.202). A `disabledMcpjsonServers` entry in any settings file rejects the server outright.

answers.primary: A `SessionStart` hook in the plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` that installs into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the per-plugin persistent directory at `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/` that survives plugin updates and is created on first reference. Use the documented pattern: `diff` the bundled `package.json` against the copy in the data directory, and on any difference copy it over and run `npm install` there; bundled scripts then resolve modules through it, for example an MCP server entry with `"NODE_PATH": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules"`.
answers.rejected_alternative: Installing `node_modules` into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` alongside the shipped code. Rejected because the plugin root path changes on every update and the superseded version directory is pruned about fourteen days later, so the installed modules are stranded and then wiped.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the SessionStart hook, creates and resolves `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, and substitutes the placeholder in hook commands and in MCP `command`/`args`/`env`. The install script owns whether the dependency state is actually correct.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs as a shell process at session start, outside the model's context; only hook output and failures cross back. The data directory is keyed to the plugin identifier and is shared across every project and session on that machine, unlike the per-version plugin root.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every session start, but the manifest diff makes it a no-op after the first successful install and re-installs only when an update ships a changed `package.json`. It stops applying when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope, at which point the data directory is deleted by default (the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts; `--keep-data` preserves it).
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and adds startup latency: if `npm install` fails, nothing blocks the session and the breakage surfaces later as module-not-found from a bundled script, which is why the documented pattern deletes the copied manifest on failure so the next session retries. The classic bug is checking only whether the directory exists, which never detects a dependency manifest changed by an update. A mid-session plugin update also keeps hook commands and MCP servers on the previous version's path until `/reload-plugins`.
answers.version_caveat: Requires a Claude Code version that supports `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, which resolves in hook and monitor commands and in MCP `command`, `args`, and `env` (and LSP `command`, `args`, `env`, `workspaceFolder`). As of v2.1.207 a hook command cannot reference `${user_config.*}` because the field is shell-parsed, so a configurable registry or token must come from the environment or a config file the script reads. Uninstall deletes the data directory unless `--keep-data` is passed.
